concepts.definition: Controls which actors or principals may perform actions on protected resources.
Creates attributable records of security-relevant or business-relevant actions and outcomes.
Schedules or executes deferred, queued, recurring, or durable work outside a request path.
Enforces request rates, concurrency bounds, or quotas over a defined key and interval.
Receives, verifies, routes, or delivers event notifications over HTTP webhook protocols.
Authorization logic linked into the application process.
Authorization enforcement integrated through framework middleware or guards.
A separately invoked policy decision component that returns authorization decisions.
A policy engine deployed beside an application and reached through a local process boundary.
A shared network service that evaluates authorization decisions for multiple applications.
A service that evaluates authorization from stored subject-resource relationships or tuples.
An adoption form that includes or requires a configurable authorization engine that evaluates a general policy model or policy language.
Authorization decisions based on controlled roles and role assignments.
Authorization decisions based on attributes of actors, resources, actions, or context.
Authorization decisions based on relationships between actors and resources.
Authorization policy represented as versionable machine-evaluated policy source.
Caching of authorization decisions or policy data under explicit invalidation behavior.
Policy isolation and modeling for multiple tenants within one deployment.
Controlled distribution or synchronization of policy bundles or policy data.
An application-integrated library that emits explicit audit events.
Middleware that captures request or application context into audit events.
An extension or plugin that records auditable activity within a database boundary.
A resident collector that receives or tails audit events for forwarding.
A pipeline component that transforms or routes audit events between producers and sinks.
A service that durably stores audit trails and exposes controlled search or query.
Audit records with controlled machine-readable fields rather than unstructured debug text.
Attachment of actor, request, tenant, or correlation context to an audit event.
Delivery behavior that retains or retries audit events across transient failures.
Search or query facilities designed for stored audit records.
Controlled retention or lifecycle behavior for audit records.
Mechanisms that make unauthorized audit-record alteration detectable.
Controlled removal, masking, or protection of sensitive audit fields.
A scheduler that runs inside the application process.
A library providing producer queues and worker execution within application-managed processes.
A job queue whose durable coordination state is stored in a database.
A job queue coordinated through a dedicated message broker.
An engine that coordinates multi-step workflows or directed acyclic task graphs.
A platform that persists execution history so long-running work can recover deterministically.
Time-based creation of work on recurring calendar or interval schedules.
Deferral of a job until a future time or delay has elapsed.
Controlled ordering preference between queued jobs.
Prevention or coalescing of duplicate queued work under a controlled identity.
Persisted state describing progress through a multi-step workflow.
Controlled creation of scheduled work missed while a scheduler was unavailable.
A rate limiter whose enforcement state is local to one application process.
A limiter that coordinates enforcement state through a shared datastore.
A network service that evaluates limits for multiple callers or gateways.
Rate-limit enforcement integrated at an API gateway or reverse proxy.
Rate-limit state and atomic enforcement implemented through datastore-side operations.
Counting requests in non-overlapping fixed time windows.
Counting or estimating requests over a continuously moving time interval.
Rate enforcement using tokens replenished at a controlled rate.
Rate smoothing through a bounded bucket drained at a controlled rate.
Virtual-scheduling rate enforcement using the generic cell rate algorithm.
A bounded allowance of operations over a defined period or allocation.
Coordinated enforcement across more than one process or node.
Explicit behavior when rate-limit state or the enforcement service is unavailable.
An endpoint or application component that receives webhook requests.
A library focused on validating webhook authenticity and integrity.
A component that sends event notifications to registered webhook endpoints.
A service that manages outbound webhook delivery and delivery state.
A gateway that receives, routes, forwards, or fans out webhook traffic.
A toolkit for interoperable webhook message, signature, or delivery conventions.
Verification of webhook message authenticity and integrity using a controlled signature scheme.
Rejection or detection of repeated signed webhook messages outside accepted replay rules.
Controlled handling that prevents repeated delivery from causing duplicate effects.
Explicit guarantees or non-guarantees about event delivery order.
Retention or routing of webhook deliveries that exhaust ordinary attempts.
Controlled transformation of outbound or routed webhook payloads.
Registration, lifecycle, secret, or status management for webhook endpoints.
Operator-triggered or policy-triggered repetition of a prior webhook delivery.
Repeated execution after failure with controlled delay or backoff behavior.
A bound on simultaneously executing jobs or admitted requests.
A Redis-compatible shared datastore.
A PostgreSQL database used for durable or coordinated state.
A dedicated broker used to queue or route messages.
A provider-operated network service outside the adopting deployment.
A continuously running worker process separate from request handling.
A separately operated component that owns policy, coordination, or configuration state.
A Kubernetes cluster required by the adoption or deployment form.
Deployed inside the adopting application process.
Deployed beside an application process with a local boundary.
Operated as a service within infrastructure controlled by the adopter.
Operated as an externally managed service.
Deployed as an API gateway, reverse-proxy, or gateway plugin.
Installed and operated as an extension within a database boundary.

ambiguities.clarificationContext: Access control may name the authorization family or a specific role-based control model.
Event logging may mean an audit capability or only a structured event feature.
Hosted service does not establish an external infrastructure dependency versus a managed deployment preference.
Job queue does not establish a library, database coordinator, or dedicated broker adoption unit.
Logging does not establish whether the request is for an audit trail or a general log pipeline.
Policy engine does not establish whether the component is a remote decision point or a locally deployed sidecar.
Task queue does not establish a library, database coordinator, or dedicated broker adoption unit.
Task runner does not establish scheduled in-process execution versus queued worker execution.
Throttling may mean concurrent-work admission or time-based request-rate enforcement.
Worker queue does not establish a library, database coordinator, or dedicated broker adoption unit.
Webhook platform does not establish delivery-service versus gateway/router responsibilities.

exclusions.explanation: Authentication establishes identity and does not alone establish authorization.
An identity provider establishes identity and does not alone define resource authorization.
JWT validation verifies a credential and does not alone enforce authorization policy.
Session management maintains identity state and does not alone establish authorization.
Formatting operational logs does not alone create an attributable audit trail.
Distributed tracing observes request flow and is not by itself an audit trail.
Metrics without attributable event records do not establish audit logging.
Broad observability does not alone establish audit-event semantics.
Generic log routing requires explicit audit-trail intent before it may resolve to the audit taxonomy.
Promise concurrency helpers do not alone provide durable queued background work.
A generic asynchronous helper does not alone provide scheduling or job coordination.
A CI workflow runner is not an application background-job adoption unit.
A build runner does not alone identify application background-job processing.
Load balancing distributes traffic and does not alone enforce a request quota.
Retry policy controls client repetition and does not alone enforce a request rate.
Local debouncing alone does not establish controlled request-rate enforcement.
A client concurrency helper without request quota enforcement is not rate limiting.
An HTTP tunnel alone does not receive, verify, route, or deliver webhooks as a product capability.
A generic HTTP client does not alone provide webhook protocol or delivery behavior.
Incidental webhook helpers in a broad SDK do not alone identify a webhook adoption unit.
Lightweight requires clarification into concrete infrastructure or deployment preferences.
Simple is subjective and does not identify a controlled capability concept.
Easy is subjective and does not identify a controlled capability concept.
Production-ready is an unsupported subjective claim rather than a controlled concept.
Enterprise is a marketing category rather than a controlled capability concept.
Scalable requires explicit workload and deployment constraints rather than an opaque label.
